claim: nrg1 levels increase after genetic ablation of approximately 50% of cardiomyocytes in the adult zebrafish ventricle.
source: Using quantitative PCR, we found that nrg1 levels increase after genetic ablation of ∼50% of cardiomyocytes in the adult zebrafish ventricle.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR measurements performed by the authors on zebrafish hearts after cardiomyocyte ablation.

claim: nrg1 levels rise above baseline at 3 days post-injury.
source: nrg1 levels rise above baseline at 3 days post-injury and peak at ∼11-fold above uninjured levels by 7 days, an injury timepoint at which cardiomyocyte proliferation also peaks (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR data showing temporal changes in nrg1 expression levels after injury.

claim: nrg1 levels peak at approximately 11-fold above uninjured levels by 7 days post-injury.
source: nrg1 levels rise above baseline at 3 days post-injury and peak at ∼11-fold above uninjured levels by 7 days, an injury timepoint at which cardiomyocyte proliferation also peaks (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR measurements showing peak nrg1 expression at 7 days post-injury.

claim: Cardiomyocyte proliferation peaks at 7 days post-injury.
source: nrg1 levels rise above baseline at 3 days post-injury and peak at ∼11-fold above uninjured levels by 7 days, an injury timepoint at which cardiomyocyte proliferation also peaks (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2011, which reported peak cardiomyocyte proliferation at 7 days post-injury.

claim: nrg1 levels lower to approximately fourfold above uninjured levels by 14 days post-injury.
source: nrg1 levels lower to ∼fourfold above uninjured levels by 14 days post injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative PCR data showing decreased but still elevated nrg1 expression at 14 days post-injury.

claim: nrg1 was rarely detectable in uninjured hearts.
source: While nrg1 was rarely detectable in uninjured hearts, nrg1 expression was induced 7 days after various injury methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAScope in situ hybridization data showing minimal nrg1 signal in uninjured hearts.

claim: nrg1 expression was induced 7 days after various injury methods.
source: While nrg1 was rarely detectable in uninjured hearts, nrg1 expression was induced 7 days after various injury methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAScope in situ hybridization data showing nrg1 expression after different types of cardiac injury.

claim: After resection of the ventricular apex, nrg1 staining was observed in small regions surrounding cardiac damage.
source: After resection of the ventricular apex, we observed nrg1 staining in small regions surrounding cardiac damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAScope in situ hybridization images showing nrg1 expression patterns after ventricular resection.

claim: After genetic cardiomyocyte ablation, larger stretches of nrg1 expression were observed distributed throughout the ventricular wall with occasional expression in the trabecular compartment.
source: We saw larger stretches of expression after genetic cardiomyocyte ablation, distributed throughout the ventricular wall with occasional expression in the trabecular compartment (Figure 1B–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAScope in situ hybridization data and images (Figure 1B-H) showing nrg1 expression patterns after genetic ablation.

claim: nrg1 signals in the ventricular wall were commonly in perivascular regions.
source: nrg1 signals in the ventricular wall were commonly in perivascular regions (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAScope in situ hybridization images (Figure 1D-F) showing nrg1 expression near blood vessels.

claim: The majority of nrg1 signals could be localized to cells also positive for tcf21:EGFP fluorescence.
source: In these experiments, the majority of nrg1 signals could be localized to cells also positive for tcf21:EGFP fluorescence (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization experiments combining RNAScope with transgenic reporter lines, shown in Figure 1I.

claim: During heart development, tcf21+ cells contribute to the epicardial layer as well as vascular support cells.
source: During heart development, tcf21+ cells contribute to the epicardial layer as well as vascular support cells (Kikuchi et al., 2011a; Acharya et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kikuchi et al., 2011a and Acharya et al., 2012, which characterized tcf21+ cell lineages.

claim: After cardiac injury, epicardial cells and their progeny proliferate and incorporate into the injury site.
source: After cardiac injury, epicardial cells and their progeny proliferate and incorporate into the injury site (Kikuchi et al., 2011a), where they have been assigned numerous pro-regenerative roles (Gemberling et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kikuchi et al., 2011a and Gemberling et al., 2013, which documented epicardial cell behavior after injury.

claim: Epicardial cells and their progeny have been assigned numerous pro-regenerative roles after cardiac injury.
source: After cardiac injury, epicardial cells and their progeny proliferate and incorporate into the injury site (Kikuchi et al., 2011a), where they have been assigned numerous pro-regenerative roles (Gemberling et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gemberling et al., 2013, which reviewed pro-regenerative roles of epicardial cells.

claim: Nrg1 is known to be expressed in Schwann cells and endothelial cells in other contexts.
source: In other contexts, Nrg1 is known to be expressed in Schwann cells and endothelial cells (Meyer et al., 1997; Cote et al., 2005; Stassart et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meyer et al., 1997, Cote et al., 2005, and Stassart et al., 2013, which documented Nrg1 expression in these cell types.

claim: nrg1 signals rarely overlapped during heart regeneration with cells positive for fli1a:EGFP or cmlc2:EGFP.
source: Yet, we found that nrg1 signals rarely overlapped during heart regeneration with cells positive for fli1a:EGFP or cmlc2:EGFP, which mark vascular endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes, respectively (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization experiments shown in Figure 1J,K using transgenic reporter lines.

claim: fli1a:EGFP marks vascular endothelial cells.
source: Yet, we found that nrg1 signals rarely overlapped during heart regeneration with cells positive for fli1a:EGFP or cmlc2:EGFP, which mark vascular endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes, respectively (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the fli1a:EGFP transgenic reporter line.

claim: cmlc2:EGFP marks cardiomyocytes.
source: Yet, we found that nrg1 signals rarely overlapped during heart regeneration with cells positive for fli1a:EGFP or cmlc2:EGFP, which mark vascular endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes, respectively (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the cmlc2:EGFP transgenic reporter line.

claim: The dominant source of nrg1 in the postnatal ventricular wall is the tcf21+ epicardial derived, perivascular cell compartment.
source: Thus, our results indicate that the dominant source of nrg1 in the postnatal ventricular wall is the tcf21+ epicardial derived, perivascular cell compartment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the colocalization data showing nrg1 expression primarily in tcf21+ cells.

claim: Messages for Nrg1 receptors Erbb2 and Erbb4b were detectable by PCR methods in uninjured adult zebrafish ventricles.
source: Messages for Nrg1 receptors Erbb2 and Erbb4b were detectable by PCR methods in uninjured adult zebrafish ventricles (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Administration of AG1478, a small molecule inhibitor of Erbb receptors, mimics the effect of erbb2 mutations on cardiac trabeculation in zebrafish.
source: Previous studies reported that the administration of AG1478, a small molecule inhibitor of Erbb receptors, mimics the effect of erbb2 mutations on cardiac trabeculation in zebrafish (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2010, which reported this finding.

claim: Treatment with 10 µM AG1478 from 6 to 7 dpa decreased cardiomyocyte proliferation by approximately 54%.
source: This regimen decreased cardiomyocyte proliferation by ∼54%, indicating that Nrg1 signaling is essential for heart regeneration (n = 20, 22; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Mef2+PCNA+ cardiomyocytes shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nrg1 signaling is essential for heart regeneration.
source: This regimen decreased cardiomyocyte proliferation by ∼54%, indicating that Nrg1 signaling is essential for heart regeneration (n = 20, 22; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that blocking Nrg1 signaling significantly reduces cardiomyocyte proliferation during regeneration.

claim: Elevated nrg1 expression led to an approximately 84% increase in the cardiomyocyte proliferation index near the injury site at 7 dpa.
source: 3 days later, we resected ventricles, and found that elevated nrg1 expression led to an ∼84% increase in the cardiomyocyte proliferation index near the injury site at 7 dpa (n = 15, 18; Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cardiomyocyte proliferation shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Elevated nrg1 expression reveals a mitogenic influence of Nrg1 signaling on heart regeneration.
source: This finding reveals a mitogenic influence of Nrg1 signaling on heart regeneration and suggests that nrg1 levels are a limiting factor for cardiomyocyte proliferation after cardiac injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that increasing nrg1 expression enhances cardiomyocyte proliferation during regeneration.

claim: nrg1 levels are a limiting factor for cardiomyocyte proliferation after cardiac injury.
source: This finding reveals a mitogenic influence of Nrg1 signaling on heart regeneration and suggests that nrg1 levels are a limiting factor for cardiomyocyte proliferation after cardiac injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that increasing nrg1 expression enhances cardiomyocyte proliferation.

claim: Within 7 days of nrg1 reactivation, there was a marked increase in cardiomyocyte proliferation, in particular within the ventricular wall.
source: Within 7 days of nrg1 reactivation, there was a marked increase in cardiomyocyte proliferation, in particular within the ventricular wall (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The cardiomyocyte proliferation index in the trabecular compartment increased modestly from approximately 0.2% to approximately 1% after 7 days of nrg1 overexpression.
source: Whereas the cardiomyocyte proliferation index in the trabecular compartment increased modestly from ∼0.2% to ∼1% after 7 days of nrg1 overexpression (Figure 3C), the proliferation index of cortical muscle increased sharply from ∼1.6% to ∼28% (n = 8, 9; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cardiomyocyte proliferation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The proliferation index of cortical muscle increased sharply from approximately 1.6% to approximately 28% after 7 days of nrg1 overexpression.
source: Whereas the cardiomyocyte proliferation index in the trabecular compartment increased modestly from ∼0.2% to ∼1% after 7 days of nrg1 overexpression (Figure 3C), the proliferation index of cortical muscle increased sharply from ∼1.6% to ∼28% (n = 8, 9; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cardiomyocyte proliferation shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Continued nrg1 overexpression over an additional 7 days maintained trabecular proliferation indices at approximately 1.6%.
source: Continued nrg1 overexpression over an additional 7 days had similar effects, maintaining trabecular proliferation indices at ∼1.6% and cortical muscle proliferation at ∼32% (n = 10, 10; Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cardiomyocyte proliferation at 14 days shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Continued nrg1 overexpression over an additional 7 days maintained cortical muscle proliferation at approximately 32%.
source: Continued nrg1 overexpression over an additional 7 days had similar effects, maintaining trabecular proliferation indices at ∼1.6% and cortical muscle proliferation at ∼32% (n = 10, 10; Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cardiomyocyte proliferation at 14 days shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The ventricular wall thickened by approximately 76% at 7 dpt compared to controls.
source: The ventricular wall thickened by ∼76% at 7 dpt compared to controls, by ∼265% at 14 dpt, and by ∼459% after 30 days of overexpression (n = 8–11; Figure 4A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ventricular wall thickness shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: The ventricular wall thickened by approximately 265% at 14 dpt compared to controls.
source: The ventricular wall thickened by ∼76% at 7 dpt compared to controls, by ∼265% at 14 dpt, and by ∼459% after 30 days of overexpression (n = 8–11; Figure 4A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ventricular wall thickness shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: The ventricular wall thickened by approximately 459% after 30 days of nrg1 overexpression.
source: The ventricular wall thickened by ∼76% at 7 dpt compared to controls, by ∼265% at 14 dpt, and by ∼459% after 30 days of overexpression (n = 8–11; Figure 4A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ventricular wall thickness shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Large increases in the number of cardiomyocyte nuclei were found within the ventricular wall after 14 days of nrg1 expression.
source: We found large increases in the number of cardiomyocyte nuclei within the ventricular wall after 14 days of nrg1 expression, and no evidence for increased cardiomyocyte size (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cardiomyocyte nuclei shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: There was no evidence for increased cardiomyocyte size after 14 days of nrg1 expression.
source: We found large increases in the number of cardiomyocyte nuclei within the ventricular wall after 14 days of nrg1 expression, and no evidence for increased cardiomyocyte size (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of cardiomyocyte area shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Most or all of the effects of nrg1 reactivation are hyperplastic.
source: Thus, most or all of the effects of nrg1 reactivation are hyperplastic.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that wall thickening is accompanied by increased cardiomyocyte numbers without increased cell size.

claim: Adult zebrafish cardiomyocytes are predominantly mononuclear.
source: To test the extent to which cellular hypertrophy contributes to this wall thickening, we assessed the size and numbers of cardiomyocytes, which are predominantly mononuclear in adult zebrafish (Wills et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wills et al., 2008, which characterized zebrafish cardiomyocyte nucleation.

claim: Animals at 6 months post-tamoxifen treatment had ventricles with an approximately 2.1-fold greater ventricular section area than control animals.
source: On average, experimental animals at 6 months post-tamoxifen treatment had ventricles with a ∼2.1-fold greater ventricular section area than control animals (n = 9, 10; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ventricular cross-sectional area shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tissue sections indicated elevated cardiomyocyte proliferation even at 6 months post-tamoxifen treatment.
source: Tissue sections indicated elevated cardiomyocyte proliferation even at this late stage, although in some cases regions of the massively thickened ventricular wall showed mild fibrin and collagen deposition (Figure 6C–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6C-G.

claim: In some cases, regions of the massively thickened ventricular wall showed mild fibrin and collagen deposition at 6 months post-tamoxifen treatment.
source: Tissue sections indicated elevated cardiomyocyte proliferation even at this late stage, although in some cases regions of the massively thickened ventricular wall showed mild fibrin and collagen deposition (Figure 6C–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFOG staining shown in Figure 6C-G.

claim: No fibrosis was detectable in hearts of animals after just 30 days of iCH.
source: No fibrosis was detectable in hearts of animals after just 30 days of iCH (n = 7; Figure 6H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFOG staining shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: Ventricular filling is altered as thickness of the ventricular walls increases.
source: These findings suggested that ventricular filling is altered as thickness of the ventricular walls increases (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from Doppler echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cardiac dysfunction was not detected at 3 months of iCH.
source: Importantly, we were unable to detect cardiac dysfunction at 3 months of iCH, and instead our results suggested that stroke volume is enhanced with iCH (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Stroke volume is enhanced with iCH at 3 months.
source: Importantly, we were unable to detect cardiac dysfunction at 3 months of iCH, and instead our results suggested that stroke volume is enhanced with iCH (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Ventricular wall hyperplasia was obvious by echocardiography by 3 months of iCH.
source: By 3 months of iCH, ventricular wall hyperplasia was obvious by echocardiography (Figure 7; Videos 1, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by echocardiography images and videos shown in Figure 7 and Videos 1, 2.

claim: Animals at 3 months of iCH showed normal endurance swimming.
source: Animals at 3 months of iCH showed normal endurance swimming, consistent with echocardiographic results.
evidence: The claim is supported by swimming endurance assay data.

claim: At later time points (8 or 9 months iCH), animals displayed a sharp reduction in swimming endurance.
source: At later time points (8 or 9 months iCH), animals displayed a sharp reduction in swimming endurance, suggesting that continued addition of myocardium eventually turns deleterious (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by swimming endurance assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Continued addition of myocardium eventually turns deleterious.
source: At later time points (8 or 9 months iCH), animals displayed a sharp reduction in swimming endurance, suggesting that continued addition of myocardium eventually turns deleterious (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that swimming endurance decreases at late time points of iCH.

claim: Forced nrg1 reactivation in the absence of cardiac injury induces robust myocardial hyperplasia in adult zebrafish.
source: Thus, forced nrg1 reactivation in the absence of cardiac injury induces robust myocardial hyperplasia in adult zebrafish, adding many new layers of myocardium over weeks of continued cardiomyocyte proliferation.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple observations of increased cardiomyocyte proliferation and wall thickening.

claim: The cortical muscle in the ventricular wall typically forms from a small number of large cardiomyocyte clones.
source: The cortical muscle in the ventricular wall typically forms from a small number of large cardiomyocyte clones.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about zebrafish heart development.

claim: Large cardiomyocyte clones expand laterally on the ventricular surface and largely retain discernable boundaries through adulthood.
source: These clones expand laterally on the ventricular surface and largely retain discernable boundaries through adulthood (Gupta and Poss, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta and Poss, 2012, which characterized cardiomyocyte clonal expansion.

claim: Regeneration of resected muscle occurs through roughly uniform proliferation by many cardiomyocytes near the injury site.
source: By contrast, regeneration of resected muscle occurs through roughly uniform proliferation by many cardiomyocytes near the injury site, generating a mixed conglomeration of small clones in the restored ventricular wall (Gupta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2013, which characterized clonal dynamics during regeneration.

claim: Regeneration of resected muscle generates a mixed conglomeration of small clones in the restored ventricular wall.
source: By contrast, regeneration of resected muscle occurs through roughly uniform proliferation by many cardiomyocytes near the injury site, generating a mixed conglomeration of small clones in the restored ventricular wall (Gupta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2013, which characterized clonal patterns during regeneration.

claim: iCH caused ectopic wall thickening by 10 wpf.
source: iCH caused ectopic wall thickening by 10 wpf, with obvious clone mixing and clone growth in the Z-plane away from the lumen (14/14 iCH, 0/11 controls; Figure 8A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by multicolor clonal analysis shown in Figure 8A-F.

claim: iCH caused obvious clone mixing and clone growth in the Z-plane away from the lumen.
source: iCH caused ectopic wall thickening by 10 wpf, with obvious clone mixing and clone growth in the Z-plane away from the lumen (14/14 iCH, 0/11 controls; Figure 8A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by multicolor clonal analysis shown in Figure 8A-F.

claim: Nrg1 does not activate a gradual layering process but builds muscle radially with proliferation dynamics that are more reminiscent of injury-induced regeneration.
source: These findings indicate that Nrg1 does not activate a gradual layering process but builds muscle radially with proliferation dynamics that are more reminiscent of injury-induced regeneration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the clonal analysis showing clone mixing rather than organized layering.

claim: After partial ventricular resection, cardiomyocytes near the injury activate regulatory sequences of the embryonic cardiogenic transcription factor gata4.
source: After partial ventricular resection, cardiomyocytes near the injury activate regulatory sequences of the embryonic cardiogenic transcription factor gata4, before dividing to create new muscle (Kikuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kikuchi et al., 2010, which characterized gata4 activation during regeneration.

claim: Gata4 activity is essential for regeneration of muscle after partial ventricular resection.
source: Moreover, Gata4 activity is essential for regeneration of this muscle (Gupta et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2013, which demonstrated the requirement for Gata4 in regeneration.

claim: 7 days of iCH in mature adults induced gata4:EGFP expression in the outermost layer of cortical muscle.
source: Using a transgenic reporter strain, we found that 7 days of iCH in mature adults induced gata4:EGFP expression in the outermost layer of cortical muscle (9/10 iCH, 1/11 controls; Figure 8G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic reporter analysis shown in Figure 8G,H.

claim: Cortical muscle displayed reduced cmlc2 expression and poorly organized sarcomeres during iCH.
source: Additionally, by coupling iCH with a transgenic reporter visualizing cardiomyocyte Actinin3 localization, we found that cortical muscle displayed reduced cmlc2 expression and poorly organized sarcomeres (Figure 8M–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic reporter analysis shown in Figure 8M-P.

claim: Reduced cmlc2 expression and poorly organized sarcomeres suggest a reduction in the contractile program that is indicative of dedifferentiation.
source: These observations together suggest a reduction in the contractile program that is indicative of dedifferentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of reduced sarcomeric organization and marker expression.

claim: iCH activated myocardial expression of tgfβ3.
source: iCH also activated myocardial expression of tgfβ3, which was implicated previously in regeneration (4/5 iCH, 0/5 controls; Figure 5I,J) (Chablais and Jazwinska, 2012; Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8I,J.

claim: tgfβ3 was implicated previously in regeneration.
source: iCH also activated myocardial expression of tgfβ3, which was implicated previously in regeneration (4/5 iCH, 0/5 controls; Figure 5I,J) (Chablais and Jazwinska, 2012; Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chablais and Jazwinska, 2012 and Choi et al., 2013.

claim: Retinoic acid synthesis in endocardial and epicardial cells is induced by myocardial injury.
source: Retinoic acid synthesis in endocardial and epicardial cells is induced by myocardial injury, where RA signaling is essential, but not sufficient, for cardiomyocyte proliferation (Kikuchi et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kikuchi et al., 2011b, which characterized RA signaling during regeneration.

claim: RA signaling is essential, but not sufficient, for cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Retinoic acid synthesis in endocardial and epicardial cells is induced by myocardial injury, where RA signaling is essential, but not sufficient, for cardiomyocyte proliferation (Kikuchi et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kikuchi et al., 2011b.

claim: Fibronectin synthesis is activated in the epicardium by injury.
source: Fibronectin (Fn) synthesis is also activated in the epicardium by injury and is an essential extracellular matrix (ECM) component of regeneration (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013, which characterized Fn during regeneration.

claim: Fibronectin is an essential extracellular matrix component of regeneration.
source: Fibronectin (Fn) synthesis is also activated in the epicardium by injury and is an essential extracellular matrix (ECM) component of regeneration (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Both raldh2 and fn1 were induced in the epicardium by 7 days of iCH.
source: Both raldh2 and fn1 were induced in the epicardium by 7 days of iCH (7 of 9 iCH, 0 of 10 controls for each marker) consistent with the presence of a regenerative program (Figure 5K,L,Q,R).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8K,L,Q,R.

claim: 7–14 days of iCH induced expansion of the epicardial layer that is reminiscent of that observed during regeneration.
source: Along with epicardial marker induction, 7–14 days of iCH induced expansion of the epicardial layer that is reminiscent of that observed during regeneration (Lepilina et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2011) (Figure 8S,T).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic reporter analysis shown in Figure 8S,T and citations to Lepilina et al., 2006 and Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Myocardial vascularization occurs concomitantly with injury-induced regeneration.
source: Finally, we assessed myocardial vascularization, which occurs concomitantly with injury-induced regeneration (Lepilina et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lepilina et al., 2006.

claim: The adult zebrafish ventricle typically has a thin muscular wall penetrated with vessels.
source: The adult zebrafish ventricle typically has a thin muscular wall penetrated with vessels, but 30 days of iCH stimulated formation of major vascular network throughout the expanded ventricular wall (Figure 8U,V).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about zebrafish heart anatomy.

claim: 30 days of iCH stimulated formation of major vascular network throughout the expanded ventricular wall.
source: The adult zebrafish ventricle typically has a thin muscular wall penetrated with vessels, but 30 days of iCH stimulated formation of major vascular network throughout the expanded ventricular wall (Figure 8U,V).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic reporter analysis shown in Figure 8U,V.

claim: After 6 months of iCH, many large coronary vessels were evident in the ventricle.
source: After 6 months of iCH, many large coronary vessels were evident in the ventricle (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Expression of a single molecule, Nrg1, is sufficient to induce and maintain critical aspects of the heart regeneration program that encompass several cell types.
source: Together, this analysis indicates that expression of a single molecule, Nrg1, is sufficient to induce and maintain critical aspects of the heart regeneration program that encompass several cell types.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple observations of regenerative hallmarks induced by Nrg1.

claim: Nrg1 is a potent activator of the heart regeneration program in zebrafish.
source: Here, we identify the extracellular factor Nrg1 as a potent activator of the heart regeneration program in zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from the entire study.

claim: Nrg1 is induced by cardiac injury.
source: Nrg1 is induced by cardiac injury and pharmacological blockade of its receptor decreases injury-induced cardiomyocyte proliferation—each indicating involvement in the endogenous process.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and RNAScope data showing nrg1 upregulation after injury.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of Nrg1 receptor decreases injury-induced cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Nrg1 is induced by cardiac injury and pharmacological blockade of its receptor decreases injury-induced cardiomyocyte proliferation—each indicating involvement in the endogenous process.
evidence: The claim is supported by AG1478 treatment experiments showing reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation.

claim: Nrg1 induction by cardiac injury and the effect of receptor blockade indicate involvement in the endogenous regeneration process.
source: Nrg1 is induced by cardiac injury and pharmacological blockade of its receptor decreases injury-induced cardiomyocyte proliferation—each indicating involvement in the endogenous process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of injury-induced expression and functional requirement.

claim: The Nrg1 protocol described is potently cardiogenic in the absence of trauma.
source: Moreover, whereas several experimental manipulations have been reported to increase cardiomyocyte proliferation in an injured adult heart, the Nrg1 protocol we describe here is potently cardiogenic in the absence of trauma.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing robust cardiomyocyte proliferation and wall thickening in uninjured hearts with Nrg1 overexpression.

claim: Nrg1 was reported to have mitogenic effects on cultured adult cardiomyocytes.
source: Nrg1 was reported to have mitogenic effects on cultured adult cardiomyocytes (Bersell et al., 2009), and its most remarkable property in our experiments was the ability to induce and maintain adult cardiomyocyte proliferation in the absence of injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bersell et al., 2009.

claim: The most remarkable property of Nrg1 in these experiments was the ability to induce and maintain adult cardiomyocyte proliferation in the absence of injury.
source: Nrg1 was reported to have mitogenic effects on cultured adult cardiomyocytes (Bersell et al., 2009), and its most remarkable property in our experiments was the ability to induce and maintain adult cardiomyocyte proliferation in the absence of injury.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the key finding from the iCH experiments.

claim: The primary cellular target of Nrg1 is likely to be cardiomyocytes.
source: Thus, the primary cellular target of Nrg1 is likely to be cardiomyocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the direct proliferative effects on cardiomyocytes and the presence of Erbb receptors in cardiomyocytes.

claim: Nrg1 effects additionally involve organizing a tissue microenvironment that includes expression of additional mitogenic factors, ECM regulation, and vascular perfusion.
source: Nrg1 effects additionally involve organizing a tissue microenvironment that includes expression of additional mitogenic factors, ECM regulation, and vascular perfusion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of epicardial activation, ECM marker induction, and vascularization during iCH.

claim: Recruitment of various non-myocyte cell types is likely to be an endogenous role of Nrg1.
source: This recruitment of various non-myocyte cell types is likely to be an endogenous role of Nrg1, given that it is also known to stimulate vascularization after ischemic injury in the hindlimb and is capable of inducing expression of ECM components in fibroblasts (Hedhli et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the current observations and supported by citations to Hedhli et al., 2012 and Kim et al., 2012.

claim: Nrg1 is known to stimulate vascularization after ischemic injury in the hindlimb.
source: This recruitment of various non-myocyte cell types is likely to be an endogenous role of Nrg1, given that it is also known to stimulate vascularization after ischemic injury in the hindlimb and is capable of inducing expression of ECM components in fibroblasts (Hedhli et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hedhli et al., 2012 and Kim et al., 2012.

claim: Nrg1 is capable of inducing expression of ECM components in fibroblasts.
source: This recruitment of various non-myocyte cell types is likely to be an endogenous role of Nrg1, given that it is also known to stimulate vascularization after ischemic injury in the hindlimb and is capable of inducing expression of ECM components in fibroblasts (Hedhli et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hedhli et al., 2012 and Kim et al., 2012.

claim: Heart regeneration is limited in adult mammals.
source: Heart regeneration is limited in adult mammals but occurs naturally in adult zebrafish through the activation of cardiomyocyte division.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mammalian cardiac regeneration capacity.

claim: Heart regeneration occurs naturally in adult zebrafish through the activation of cardiomyocyte division.
source: Heart regeneration is limited in adult mammals but occurs naturally in adult zebrafish through the activation of cardiomyocyte division.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about zebrafish cardiac regeneration.

claim: Neuregulin1 (Nrg1) was previously shown to have mitogenic effects on mammalian cardiomyocytes.
source: In this study, we find evidence that Neuregulin1 (Nrg1), previously shown to have mitogenic effects on mammalian cardiomyocytes, is sharply induced in perivascular cells after injury to the adult zebrafish heart.
evidence: The claim references previous literature on Nrg1's mitogenic effects.

claim: Nrg1 is sharply induced in perivascular cells after injury to the adult zebrafish heart.
source: In this study, we find evidence that Neuregulin1 (Nrg1), previously shown to have mitogenic effects on mammalian cardiomyocytes, is sharply induced in perivascular cells after injury to the adult zebrafish heart.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and RNAScope data showing nrg1 induction in perivascular cells after injury.

claim: Inhibition of Erbb2, an Nrg1 co-receptor, disrupts cardiomyocyte proliferation in response to injury.
source: Inhibition of Erbb2, an Nrg1 co-receptor, disrupts cardiomyocyte proliferation in response to injury, whereas myocardial Nrg1 overexpression enhances this proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by AG1478 treatment experiments showing reduced cardiomyocyte proliferation.

claim: Myocardial Nrg1 overexpression enhances cardiomyocyte proliferation in response to injury.
source: Inhibition of Erbb2, an Nrg1 co-receptor, disrupts cardiomyocyte proliferation in response to injury, whereas myocardial Nrg1 overexpression enhances this proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing increased cardiomyocyte proliferation after injury in Nrg1-overexpressing animals.

claim: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation.
source: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, overt muscle hyperplasia, epicardial activation, increased vascularization, and causes cardiomegaly through persistent addition of wall myocardium.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of reduced sarcomeric organization and gata4 activation in uninjured hearts with Nrg1 overexpression.

claim: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces overt muscle hyperplasia.
source: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, overt muscle hyperplasia, epicardial activation, increased vascularization, and causes cardiomegaly through persistent addition of wall myocardium.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased cardiomyocyte numbers and wall thickening.

claim: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces epicardial activation.
source: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, overt muscle hyperplasia, epicardial activation, increased vascularization, and causes cardiomegaly through persistent addition of wall myocardium.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing epicardial marker induction and expansion.

claim: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces increased vascularization.
source: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, overt muscle hyperplasia, epicardial activation, increased vascularization, and causes cardiomegaly through persistent addition of wall myocardium.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased vascular networks in the thickened ventricular wall.

claim: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression causes cardiomegaly through persistent addition of wall myocardium.
source: In uninjured zebrafish, the reactivation of Nrg1 expression induces cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation, overt muscle hyperplasia, epicardial activation, increased vascularization, and causes cardiomegaly through persistent addition of wall myocardium.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased ventricular size and wall thickness over time.

claim: Nrg1 is a potent, induced mitogen for the endogenous adult heart regeneration program.
source: Our findings identify Nrg1 as a potent, induced mitogen for the endogenous adult heart regeneration program.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion from the entire study.

claim: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a common injury that causes permanent loss of hundreds of millions of cardiac muscle cells.
source: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a common injury that causes permanent loss of hundreds of millions of cardiac muscle cells, increasing susceptibility to heart failure and sudden death.
evidence: The claim is based on established medical knowledge about myocardial infarction.

claim: Myocardial infarction increases susceptibility to heart failure and sudden death.
source: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a common injury that causes permanent loss of hundreds of millions of cardiac muscle cells, increasing susceptibility to heart failure and sudden death.
evidence: The claim is based on established medical knowledge about consequences of MI.

claim: New myocardium is created through division of spared cardiomyocytes during zebrafish heart regeneration.
source: New myocardium is created through division of spared cardiomyocytes, and lineage-tracing experiments have not yielded evidence for a stem cell contribution (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jopling et al., 2010 and Kikuchi et al., 2010.

claim: Lineage-tracing experiments have not yielded evidence for a stem cell contribution to zebrafish heart regeneration.
source: New myocardium is created through division of spared cardiomyocytes, and lineage-tracing experiments have not yielded evidence for a stem cell contribution (Jopling et al., 2010; Kikuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jopling et al., 2010 and Kikuchi et al., 2010.

claim: Zebrafish regenerate after injuries that deplete 60% or more of their cardiomyocytes.
source: Zebrafish regenerate after injuries that deplete 60% or more of their cardiomyocytes, suggesting broad potential of most or all cardiomyocytes to participate in regeneration in these animals (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The ability of zebrafish to regenerate after severe injury suggests broad potential of most or all cardiomyocytes to participate in regeneration.
source: Zebrafish regenerate after injuries that deplete 60% or more of their cardiomyocytes, suggesting broad potential of most or all cardiomyocytes to participate in regeneration in these animals (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that zebrafish can regenerate after severe cardiomyocyte depletion.

claim: Cardiomyocyte division is robust through early postnatal life in mice and can enable regeneration.
source: By contrast, cardiomyocyte division is robust through early postnatal life in mice and can enable regeneration, but by the adult stage is profoundly reduced (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Porrello et al., 2011.

claim: By the adult stage, cardiomyocyte division in mice is profoundly reduced.
source: By contrast, cardiomyocyte division is robust through early postnatal life in mice and can enable regeneration, but by the adult stage is profoundly reduced (Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Porrello et al., 2011.

claim: The adult heart is famously resistant to forced hyperplasia.
source: The adult heart is famously resistant to forced hyperplasia, and tumors of myocardial origin are exceedingly rare.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cardiac biology.

claim: Tumors of myocardial origin are exceedingly rare.
source: The adult heart is famously resistant to forced hyperplasia, and tumors of myocardial origin are exceedingly rare.
evidence: The claim is based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Adult mammalian cardiomyocyte proliferation has been reported to be stimulated to a minor extent after ischemic injury.
source: Adult mammalian cardiomyocyte proliferation has been reported to be stimulated to a minor extent after ischemic injury (Senyo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Senyo et al., 2013.

claim: Genetic manipulations in cardiomyocytes of cell cycle genes like cyclin D, Rb, and/or p130 can increase cardiomyocyte cell cycle entry or division but do not cause significant muscularization.
source: Genetic manipulations in cardiomyocytes of cell cycle genes like cyclin D, Rb, and/or p130 can increase cardiomyocyte cell cycle entry or division but do not cause significant muscularization (Pasumarthi et al., 2005; Sdek et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pasumarthi et al., 2005 and Sdek et al., 2011.

claim: Manipulations of Hippo signaling or miRNA function can increase cardiomyocyte proliferation after injury in mice.
source: Similarly, manipulations of Hippo signaling or miRNA function can increase cardiomyocyte proliferation after injury in mice (Eulalio et al., 2012; Heallen et al., 2013; Xin et al., 2013), but no compelling evidence for an impact on adult cardiogenesis has been reported.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eulalio et al., 2012, Heallen et al., 2013, and Xin et al., 2013.

claim: No compelling evidence for an impact on adult cardiogenesis has been reported for manipulations of Hippo signaling or miRNA function.
source: Similarly, manipulations of Hippo signaling or miRNA function can increase cardiomyocyte proliferation after injury in mice (Eulalio et al., 2012; Heallen et al., 2013; Xin et al., 2013), but no compelling evidence for an impact on adult cardiogenesis has been reported.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: In adult zebrafish, several manipulations have boosted cardiomyocyte proliferation after trauma.
source: In adult zebrafish, several manipulations have boosted cardiomyocyte proliferation after trauma (Jopling et al., 2012; Yin et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2013), yet no genetic or pharmacologic method has stimulated cardiomyocyte proliferation or obvious cardiogenic growth in the absence of injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jopling et al., 2012, Yin et al., 2012, and Choi et al., 2013.

claim: No genetic or pharmacologic method has stimulated cardiomyocyte proliferation or obvious cardiogenic growth in the absence of injury in adult zebrafish prior to this study.
source: In adult zebrafish, several manipulations have boosted cardiomyocyte proliferation after trauma (Jopling et al., 2012; Yin et al., 2012; Choi et al., 2013), yet no genetic or pharmacologic method has stimulated cardiomyocyte proliferation or obvious cardiogenic growth in the absence of injury.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Nrg1 signaling is critical for cardiac myofiber trabeculation in developing zebrafish or mouse embryos.
source: In developing zebrafish or mouse embryos, Nrg1 signaling is critical for cardiac myofiber trabeculation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Nrg1's developmental roles.

claim: Mice mutant in Nrg1, or in its receptors ErbB2 or ErbB4, die at mid-gestation, or later with cardiac-restricted mutations, from thin ventricular walls and aberrant trabeculation.
source: Mice mutant in Nrg1, or in its receptors ErbB2 or ErbB4, die at mid-gestation, or later with cardiac-restricted mutations, from thin ventricular walls and aberrant trabeculation (Gassmann et al., 1995; Lee et al., 1995; Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gassmann et al., 1995, Lee et al., 1995, Meyer and Birchmeier, 1995, and Liu et al., 2010.

claim: Nrg1 delivery to embryonic mouse cardiac explants or embryonic rat cardiomyocytes increased their proliferation in culture.
source: Nrg1 delivery to embryonic mouse cardiac explants or embryonic rat cardiomyocytes increased their proliferation in culture (Zhao et al., 1998), and Nrg1 treatment of cultured adult mouse cardiomyocytes or systemic injection into adult mice induced cardiomyocyte proliferation (Bersell et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 1998.

claim: Nrg1 treatment of cultured adult mouse cardiomyocytes or systemic injection into adult mice induced cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Nrg1 delivery to embryonic mouse cardiac explants or embryonic rat cardiomyocytes increased their proliferation in culture (Zhao et al., 1998), and Nrg1 treatment of cultured adult mouse cardiomyocytes or systemic injection into adult mice induced cardiomyocyte proliferation (Bersell et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bersell et al., 2009.

claim: Nrg1 injection improves cardiac repair after MI.
source: Although the proliferative increases in this latter study were relatively small, the authors also found evidence that Nrg1 injection improves cardiac repair after MI.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from Bersell et al., 2009.

claim: Nrg1 has reported effects on cell survival, metabolism, angiogenesis, and myofiber structure in addition to cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Nrg1 has reported effects on cell survival, metabolism, angiogenesis, and myofiber structure in addition to cardiomyocyte proliferation (Parodi and Kuhn, 2014), influences that are possibly reflected by functional improvement after Nrg1 infusion in congestive heart failure patients (Jabbour et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parodi and Kuhn, 2014.

claim: Functional improvement after Nrg1 infusion in congestive heart failure patients possibly reflects Nrg1's effects on cell survival, metabolism, angiogenesis, and myofiber structure.
source: Nrg1 has reported effects on cell survival, metabolism, angiogenesis, and myofiber structure in addition to cardiomyocyte proliferation (Parodi and Kuhn, 2014), influences that are possibly reflected by functional improvement after Nrg1 infusion in congestive heart failure patients (Jabbour et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting clinical observations to potential mechanisms.

claim: A recent study argued that Nrg1 delivery to adult mice has no effects on cardiomyocyte proliferation.
source: Indeed, a recent study argued that Nrg1 delivery to adult mice has no effects on cardiomyocyte proliferation (Reuter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reuter et al., 2014.
